"executive_summary": "This paper provides a structured survey of image noise types and a comparative analysis of image denoising algorithms, culminating in a quantitative evaluation on a single noisy image. The authors argue that noise degrades image quality and appearance, and that selecting an appropriate denoising algorithm is application-dependent, requiring knowledge of the noise present. They classify noise into additive and multiplicative categories, describing Gaussian, Salt and Pepper, Speckle, and Brownian noise with their mathematical models and visual illustrations. The paper then presents a classification of denoising algorithms into spatial filtering (linear and non-linear) and transform domain filtering (spatial-frequency and wavelet domain), detailing sub-approaches such as thresholding methods, non-orthogonal wavelet transforms, and wavelet coefficient modeling. Performance is measured using PSNR and IEF, with results reported for six filters on a 90% noise-density grayscale Lena image. The main finding is that MDBUTMF achieves the best performance (PSNR 17.9865, IEF 16.2066), outperforming mean, adaptive mean, and PSMF filters, while wavelet-based methods (DBA, MDBA) substantially outperform simple spatial filters. The paper concludes with promising directions for future research. However, the study is limited by its reliance on a single image and a single noise density, the absence of a formal experimental methodology section, and the lack of reported hardware, hyperparameters, or reproducibility details. The paper serves as a foundational reference for understanding denoising taxonomy and relative filter performance, though its quantitative claims should be interpreted cautiously given the narrow evaluation scope.",

summary.title: Comparative Performance Analysis of Image De-noising Techniques
summary.authors: Vivek Kumar, Pranay Yadav, Atul Samadhiya, Sandeep Jain, and Prayag Tiwari
summary.executive_summary: This paper provides a structured survey of image noise types and a comparative analysis of image denoising algorithms, culminating in a quantitative evaluation on a single noisy image. The authors argue that noise degrades image quality and appearance, and that selecting an appropriate denoising algorithm is application-dependent, requiring knowledge of the noise present. They classify noise into additive and multiplicative categories, describing Gaussian, Salt and Pepper, Speckle, and Brownian noise with their mathematical models and visual illustrations. The paper then presents a classification of denoising algorithms into spatial filtering (linear and non-linear) and transform domain filtering (spatial-frequency and wavelet domain), detailing sub-approaches such as thresholding methods, non-orthogonal wavelet transforms, and wavelet coefficient modeling. Performance is measured using PSNR and IEF, with results reported for six filters on a 90% noise-density grayscale Lena image. The main finding is that MDBUTMF achieves the best performance (PSNR 17.9865, IEF 16.2066), outperforming mean, adaptive mean, and PSMF filters, while wavelet-based methods (DBA, MDBA) substantially outperform simple spatial filters. The paper concludes with promising directions for future research. However, the study is limited by its reliance on a single image and a single noise density, the absence of a formal experimental methodology section, and the lack of reported hardware, hyperparameters, or reproducibility details. The paper serves as a foundational reference for understanding denoising taxonomy and relative filter performance, though its quantitative claims should be interpreted cautiously given the narrow evaluation scope.
